summary: An independent check of Vehicles, Big purchase planner and Renovation found five ways their money figures were wrong, and all five are fixed. The biggest: leasing a new car looked dearer by the whole trade-in value of your current car, and paying cash for a purchase took the full price even when part was already saved.
points: Vehicles: keeping your car now counts what its loan still owes at the end, as buying and leasing do when they pay it off at the start.
Vehicles: leasing now credits what your current car is worth over its loan, as buying already did.
Big purchase planner: paying cash takes only what is not already set aside, which is what the screen showed all along.
Renovation: a cash-out refinance fits only up to 80% of the home's value, closing costs included, and a cheaper refinance can now show the tax deduction it gives up.
Renovation: interest on home debt past $750,000 ($375,000 filing separately), and on closing costs rolled into a refinance, no longer counts as deductible.
numbers: 1,249 of 1,500 sample lease comparisons were too dear (by $12,000 in one worked example)
1,140 of 1,500 sample cash purchases took too much from savings
80% of the home's value: the usual cash-out refinance limit (HUD)

shots.caption: A sample family's sedan over 2 years: keeping it counts the $5,557 still owed on its loan, and the lease takes off the $9,800 the car brings in.
A $35,000 kitchen for an itemizing household: the line's tax saving is counted, and the refinance says it would be 81% of the home's value, over the usual 80%.
